thread:
Brian Murphy: quick check-in on changelog endpoints before I lock the API contract. We need to align on pagination + filtering semantics *and* what we’re going to cache (console vs public feed). Anyone have strong opinions on cursor vs offset?

Chloe Martin: please no offset. we’re going to have “published” entries being inserted + corrected/superseded, so offset will drift and UI will get dupes/missing items.

Ethan Park: +1 cursor. control plane already does cursor for most list endpoints.

Michael Nguyen: cursor is also easier for deterministic ordering once we add “multiple changes same day” fix. tie-breaker needs to be in the cursor.

Brian Murphy: ok. proposal:
- `GET /v1/model-changelog/entries`
- supports filters: `model_id`, `version_id`, `change_type` (added|updated|deprecated|superseded), `state` (draft|in_review|published), `published_after`, `published_before`
- ordering: `published_at DESC, event_id DESC` (event_id is monotonic-ish per source, but we can treat as a lexicographic tie-breaker)
- pagination: `limit` (default 20, max 100) + `page_token` (opaque)
- response includes `next_page_token`

Chloe Martin: for console UI, we also need “show me everything for this model, newest first” + ability to filter to a version. the above covers.

Jada Williams: state default should be `published` unless explicitly asked. drafts shouldn’t be fetchable w/out auth + role.

Brian Murphy: yup. default `state=published`. console will call with auth + can request drafts.

Logan Wright: caching question: public feed endpoint will get hammered by customers polling. we should strongly define cache semantics. are we doing ETags?

Brian Murphy: I was thinking:
- For the public endpoint (no auth): `Cache-Control: public, max-age=60, stale-while-revalidate=300`
- `ETag` per query+page (or at least per query without page? tricky)
- Support `If-None-Match` -> 304

Ethan Park: per page token caching is fine; page tokens should be stable for a given ordering. but if we publish new entries, page 1 changes and old page 2 tokens might now represent different windows unless the cursor is “after <published_at,event_id>”.

Michael Nguyen: yeah cursor should encode the last item seen: `(published_at,event_id)` in the ordering. then “give me entries with (published_at,event_id) < cursor” in DESC order. that makes old tokens stable even as new things appear at the top.

Brian Murphy: exactly. page_token will be base64 of JSON like `{"published_at":"2024-01-27T19:20:11Z","event_id":"evt_01H..."}` but opaque to clients.

Chloe Martin: pls don’t leak internal ids in the token if we can avoid? (docs team paranoia about customers screenshotting it)

Brian Murphy: token is opaque; but yes, it will contain event_id. we can encrypt/sign it instead of plain base64 if we care. encrypt might be overkill but signing is probably needed so clients can’t tamper.

Ethan Park: we already have a standard for this in control plane (`SignedCursorV1`). it’s HMAC signed + base64. not encrypted but prevents tampering. (still “decodable” if you try).

Logan Wright: if we do non-encrypted, assume customers can decode. not necessarily bad, but we should be ok with event_id being “public-ish”. if not ok, we need encryption.

Michael Nguyen: I think event_id in the cursor is fine as long as event_id itself isn’t meaningful. it’s basically a UUID. the bigger concern is if cursor included internal model nickname or actor.

Brian Murphy: agreed; cursor payload will only include `published_at` + `entry_id` (not actor, not model). entry_id is stable and already in the response anyway.

Chloe Martin: +1, “entry_id” not “event_id”. the response already includes entry_id so it’s not new data.

Brian Murphy: ok, updated: cursor uses `(published_at, entry_id)`.

Jada Williams: filtering semantics question: what happens if client supplies `published_after` + `page_token`? do we ignore one?

Brian Murphy: good point. I’d rather validate:
- if `page_token` is set, other filters *must* match the ones encoded in the token OR request 400.
- easiest is to encode a hash of canonical query params in the token and validate.

Ethan Park: yep. otherwise clients accidentally mix params and get weird gaps.

Chloe Martin: console will do infinite scrolling; we can keep it consistent.

Logan Wright: caching + query params: for CDN caching we need to keep query space small. do we really need both `published_after/before` for public? customers asked for “since last check”.

Brian Murphy: public feed can support `published_after` only (since) and `limit`. `published_before` is mainly for console/backfill use.

Michael Nguyen: +1. also: “since” should be inclusive or exclusive? we should define. I vote exclusive (`>`) to avoid duplicate last entry.

Brian Murphy: ok:
- `published_after` is exclusive (return entries with `published_at` strictly greater than param)
- For pagination cursor comparison is also exclusive using last seen tuple.

Chloe Martin: and ordering is always desc. so for “since” you still get newest first; they can keep polling.

Logan Wright: for public caching, if they pass `published_after=...` that’s basically uncacheable because it varies per client.

Brian Murphy: true, but “public feed” for customers will likely use either:
- no params (latest page)
- or the Atom/RSS endpoint which is cached
The JSON endpoint can be cached only on common queries; customers who pass “since” will bypass most cache.

Ethan Park: we should document that for high-frequency polling, better use ETag on the unparameterized latest page.

Logan Wright: +1 and add a rate limit. if we do ETag correctly, well-behaved clients will see mostly 304s.

Brian Murphy: noted. caching strategy summary:
- Console/authenticated endpoints: no CDN caching; internal service-level cache in Redis (30s) keyed by query, to protect DB.
- Public unauth JSON feed: CDN cache for latest page (60s) + ETag + 304; strict max limit (50?)
- RSS/Atom: CDN cache longer (5m) since it’s for humans.

Chloe Martin: what about “superseded” entries? does listing include both original and corrected? UI needs to show corrections.

Michael Nguyen: behavior we discussed in generator PR: when a published entry is corrected, we create a new entry with `change_type=superseded` and link to `supersedes_entry_id`. customers should see both, with the older one marked “superseded”.

Brian Murphy: API can include `status` field like `active|superseded` and `superseded_by_entry_id` (nullable). That way list endpoints don’t hide history.

Jada Williams: and filters: default should include superseded entries? I’d prefer yes, but UI can collapse.

Chloe Martin: console can collapse by default (show a “Corrected on …” banner) but we need them accessible.

Brian Murphy: default includes them. optional filter `include_superseded=false` for folks who just want the latest signal.

Logan Wright: please make sure cache keys include that flag.

Ethan Park: +1 and `Vary` headers if we do any content negotiation.

Brian Murphy: cool. I’ll capture in the API doc and align with control plane conventions. next step I’ll push a short spec snippet into the Confluence page + link here for async review.

Chloe Martin: :thumbsup: when you have it, I’ll sanity check it against console requirements (filters + paging).

Logan Wright: drop me the headers you plan (Cache-Control/ETag). I want to make sure it works with our edge cache + doesn’t kill observability.

Michael Nguyen: and pls make sure ordering uses `(published_at, entry_id)` deterministic. we already got burned by “same day collapse” in staging.

Brian Murphy: yep. ordering + cursor tie-breaker is explicitly that tuple. will follow up w/ a draft link.
